DAPR3 2627 Report - what we would do

Very first thing is just take a look at the data:

library(tidyverse)
library(patchwork)
library(lme4)
library(lmerTest)
library(effects)
library(broom.mixed)
library(HLMdiag)

wally <- read_csv('https://uoepsy.github.io/dapr3/2627/report/dapr3_2627_report.csv')
head(wally)
# A tibble: 6 × 7
  ppt    group   age platform scene      n_chars TOTAL_FIXATIONS
  <chr>  <dbl> <dbl> <chr>    <chr>        <dbl>           <dbl>
1 PID001     1    19 iOS      Beach          300              36
2 PID001     1    19 iOS      Ski Resort     300              36
3 PID001     1    19 iOS      Fairground     300              32
4 PID001     1    NA <NA>     Airport         NA              NA
5 PID001     1    19 iOS      Wild West      350              50
6 PID001     1    19 iOS      Stone Age      350              42
contrasts e-scaling the n_chars variable

Let’s change things to factors, specifically the group variable. We’re going to want to compare everything against “standard”, because that’s how the predictions are framed, so let’s set that as the reference level.

wally <- 
  wally |> mutate(
    group = factor(group, levels=c(2,1,3),
                   labels = c("standard","desaturated","gridoverlay")),
    platform = factor(platform),
    scene = factor(scene)
  )

I’m also going to re-scale then_chars predictor, so that it coefficients reflect change in fixations for every 100 additional characters (rather than every additional 1). I’ll also center it on 300, the least busy scene.

You don’t have to do this re-scaling right at the outset. It will probably help model convergence later on. Alternatively, you could leave it as is and re-scale it if needed for the model. And you don’t have to do this specific scaling, you could just Z-score it - the important thing is keeping track (and being clear in communication) about what “0” means on the scale, and what “moving 1” represents.

wally <- 
  wally |> 
  mutate(
    # recenter on 300, scale to 100-characters
    n_chars = (n_chars/100) - 3
  )

exploring what predictors varies by which groups

To help me keep track of what could be in random effects etc, I like to plot things facetted by the groups. We have both groupings of both participants and scenes here.

We could do tables here instead, like we’ve seen (using xtabs() but really it’s all just the same idea of seeing what predictors vary between groups and what predictors vary within groups).

If we plot n_chars on the x, and TOTAL_FIXATIONS on the y, we can see that this varies within participants, but between scenes:

ggplot(wally, aes(x=n_chars, y=TOTAL_FIXATIONS))+
  geom_point()+
  facet_wrap(~ppt)+
  labs(title="participants") +
  
  ggplot(wally, aes(x=n_chars, y=TOTAL_FIXATIONS))+
  geom_point()+
  facet_wrap(~scene)+
  labs(title="scenes")

And if we do the same for the group (standard, desaturated, gridoverlay), it’s the other way around:

ggplot(wally, aes(x=group, y=TOTAL_FIXATIONS))+
  geom_boxplot()+
  facet_wrap(~ppt)+
  labs(title="participants") +
  
  ggplot(wally, aes(x=group, y=TOTAL_FIXATIONS))+
  geom_boxplot()+
  facet_wrap(~scene)+
  labs(title="scenes")

(I’d probably want to tidy up the axes so they are readable if I plan on showing a reader these plots, but they’re really just for my own exploration here)

building a model

Let’s make a model!

We’re interested in TOTAL_FIXATIONS ~ n_chars * group.
this is whether the change in fixations as a scene gets busier (n_chars) is different depending on which condition people are in (desaturated, colour, etc).

We have multiple observations per person, and multiple observations per scene. n_chars varies between the scenes, but within people, and the group varies between people but within scenes.

So we can try this:

mod_wally <- 
  lmer(TOTAL_FIXATIONS ~ 1 + n_chars * group +
       (1 + n_chars | ppt) + 
       (1 + group | scene),  
     data = wally)

And it converges! hooray!

Note that if we hadn’t re-scaled n_chars, then it probably throws an error.

# undoing the transformation we did earlier:  
wally <- wally |>
  mutate(
    n_chars_original = (n_chars + 3)* 100
  )

mod_wally_noscale <- 
  lmer(TOTAL_FIXATIONS ~ 1 + n_chars_original * group +
       (1 + n_chars_original | ppt) + 
       (1 + group | scene),  
     data = wally)

We could just as easily use a z-scored version of n_chars, it would then converge

wally <- wally |>
  mutate(
    n_chars_z = (n_chars - mean(n_chars, na.rm=TRUE))/sd(n_chars, na.rm=TRUE)
  )

mod_wally_z <- 
  lmer(TOTAL_FIXATIONS ~ 1 + n_chars_z * group +
       (1 + n_chars_z | ppt) + 
       (1 + group | scene),  
     data = wally)

there’s a slight disadvantage to z-scoring here. For interpretation, it’s useful to know what “0” and “moving 1” mean in reality - i.e., in the context of the experiment.

mean(wally$n_chars_original)
[1] 401.3889
sd(wally$n_chars_original)
[1] 71.18722

What this means is that some of our fixed effects coefficients will be specifically for scenes with 401.4 characters in them (I’m kind of fine with just saying ~400). It will also mean that some of the coefficients tell us the change in average fixations when we add 71.2 characters.
That feels a bit odd to me?
And if we forget to tell the reader what 0 and 1 now mean, they’ll never actually know that it is “adding 71.2 characters”..

what about age and platform?

Not everything in the data needs to be in the model. Because we are running a randomised experiment here, where everyone sees all of the n_chars values, and people are randomly allocated into the conditions (desaturated, standard, grid-overlay), it means that whether we include/exclude things like age and platform will not bias our estimates. It would only become a problem if something like age influenced what condition people are in (and also influenced their visual search efficiency).
So essentially - this model would also be fine:

mod_wally_covars <- 
  lmer(TOTAL_FIXATIONS ~ 1 + age + platform + n_chars * group +
       (1 + n_chars | ppt) + 
       (1 + group | scene),  
     data = wally)

# note that the effects we are interested in haven't changed much: 
fixef(mod_wally)
             (Intercept)                  n_chars         groupdesaturated 
               36.837781                 9.971552                 3.352932 
        groupgridoverlay n_chars:groupdesaturated n_chars:groupgridoverlay 
               -7.343313                -4.980792                -5.988778 
fixef(mod_wally_covars)
             (Intercept)                      age          platformWindows 
             37.72278647              -0.03384212              -0.56238755 
                 n_chars         groupdesaturated         groupgridoverlay 
              9.97165039               3.26300058              -7.35295866 
n_chars:groupdesaturated n_chars:groupgridoverlay 
             -4.98117561              -5.98729077

what we probably don’t want to try, is putting age and platform in as grouping variables like

..... (1 + .... | age ) + (1 + ..... | platform)

Why not? although age captures groups (18,19,20,…) and so on, any variability this creates in the outcome we would expect to be reproducible (such that higher values tend to correspond with less efficient search). So even if we get different groups the next time round (we could get 26,27,28, year olds), this would lead to the same systematic influence on visual search (higher age, poorer searching). So if we want to include age in the model, it would be much more appropriate to think of it as a reproducible slope such that “1 year older >> X more fixations”, rather than “the randomly sample age group you are in will have a higher/lower nr fixations”.

Similarly, if there are any platform differences in visual search efficiency, then we would expect these to come out again if we repeated the experiment on a new sample (we would still get Windows & iOS users, and still get the avg differences between the platforms). On a more practical note, there are only 2 levels here, and using a random effect (1 | g) tries to estimate a variance across the levels of g. Estimating a variance in 2 groups is actually just the same thing as estimating the difference.

assumptions etc?

Residual plots look okay. some of the scene random slopes are a bit off, but there are only 20 scenes, so maybe this isn’t too bad..

and check for influence:

inf_obs  <- hlm_influence(model = mod_wally, level = 1, approx = TRUE)
inf_ppt <- hlm_influence(model = mod_wally, level = "ppt", approx = TRUE)
inf_scene <- hlm_influence(model = mod_wally, level = "scene", approx = TRUE)

dotplot_diag(inf_obs$cooksd, cutoff="internal") + 
dotplot_diag(inf_ppt$cooksd, index=inf_ppt$ppt, cutoff="internal") +
dotplot_diag(inf_scene$cooksd, index=inf_ppt$scene, cutoff="internal")

visualising the model

Okay, I’m happy with the model, so let’s do some visualising.

Quick and easy would be:

library(sjPlot)
plot_model(mod_wally, type = "int")

I’ve gone a bit more involved here than is probably necessary, and added the participant-level average fitted values in as well as the fixed effects:

pfix <- effect("n_chars*group", mod_wally) |>
  as.data.frame()

augment(mod_wally) |>
  group_by(group, ppt, n_chars) |>
  summarise(
    .fitted = mean(.fitted)
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = n_chars, col=group)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = .fitted, group = ppt), alpha=.3) +
  geom_line(data = pfix, 
            aes(y = fit, col = group)) +
  geom_ribbon(data = pfix,
              aes(ymin=lower,ymax=upper,fill=group), 
              col=NA, alpha=.3) +
  scale_fill_viridis_d(option="A",begin=0,end=.7) + 
  scale_color_viridis_d(option="A",begin=0,end=.7) +
  theme_minimal()+
  scale_x_continuous(
    "Number of characters",
    breaks = seq(0,2,.5),
    labels = seq(300,500,50))+
  labs(y="Model predicted fixation count")

Fixed effects

Here’s what each of our coefficients represent.

  • Intercept: estimated avg nr fixations for scenes with 300 characters, viewed in standard condition
    • key here is what “0” means in n_chars, and what the reference level of group is.
    • it’s the height of the black line at the left hand edge of Figure 1
  • n_chars: estimated change in avg nr fixations for every 100 characters more busy a scene is, when in the standard condition.
    • key to this is that it is specifically in the “standard” condition
    • it’s the slope of the black line in Figure 1
  • groupdesaturated: estimated difference in avg fixations between standard and desaturated scenes with 300 characters
    • key here is that it’s comparing desaturated with standard, and that it is specifically at “0” on n_chars (whatever “0” means in our scaling)
    • it’s the difference in the height at the left hand edge of Figure 1, between the purple line and the black line
  • groupgridoverlay: estimated difference in avg fixations between standard and grid overlay scenes with 300 characters
    • key here is that it’s comparing grid overlay with standard, and that it is specifically at “0” on n_chars (whatever “0” means in our scaling)
    • it’s the difference in the height at the left hand edge of Figure 1, between the orange line and the black line
  • nchars:desaturated: compared to the 9.97 increase in fixations for every 100 additional characters for scenes viewed in “standard”, the “desaturated” scenes increase by -4.98 fewer fixations.
    • wording of interactions is always tricky, but the key things are that it is the comparison between desaturated and standard, and that it is comparing the increase. so the -4.98 is an adjustment to the slope in the standard condition.
    • the slope of the purple line compared to the slope of the black line in Figure 1
  • nchars:gridoverlay: compared to the 9.97 increase in fixations for every 100 additional characters for scenes viewed in “standard”, the “desaturated” scenes increase by -5.99 fewer fixations.
    • it is the comparison between gridoverlay and standard, and it is comparing the increase in fixations for every 100 characters between the two conditions.
    • the slope of the orange line compared to the slope of the black line in Figure 1

random effects

Lots of different ways we can talk about random effects, here’s the main points that come out to me.
We definitely don’t have to talk about all of these!

  • both ppts and scenes show similar variability (intercept variation is similar: 5.29 and 4.26, around the fixed intercept of ~37)
  • effect of n_chars varies by ppt. in standard condition the 95% people will have slopes between ~4.93 and 15.01 (\(9.97 \pm (2 \times 2.52)\))
  • people who make more fixations for least busy scenes tend to increase less as the n_chars increases (this is the -0.35 correlation)
    • this is actually more difficult to interpret if you Z-scored n_chars, because we’re saying ‘people who make more fixations for the average n_chars (~425ish characters), tend to increase more for busier scenes’. This kind of makes sense because by 425 characters people who make more fixations have already been influenced by the increasing business!
  • grid overlay tends to reduce fixations for all scenes
    • at 300 characters (the intercept), this is \(-7.34 \pm (2 \times 2.47)\)
    • as nr characters increases, the -7.34 difference gets bigger (the orange and black lines in Figure 1 get farther apart)
  • desaturation much more mixed
    • we actually can already sort of see this because at 300 characters (the intercept), it is positive, but by 500 characters the desaturated condition is lower than standard.
  • scenes creating more fixations in the standard condition tended to show greater reductions in desaturated & grid overlay (these are the -0.55 and -.17 correlations)
  • scenes where desaturation had less of a reduction (relative to standard) in fixations tended to have greater improvements with grid overlay (relative to standard) (this is the -0.73 correlation)
Findings

So we have an overarching research question:

RQ: Does the decrease in visual search efficiency due to number of distractor characters differ between the three conditions?

And 3 specific predictions to talk about:

  1. In the “standard colour” condition, people will be less efficient at visually searching scenes with greater numbers of characters.
  2. The effect of character number could plausibly be smaller in the “grid overlay” condition, because the grid might help people search systematically.
  3. The effect of character number could plausibly be larger in the “desaturated” condition, because removing colour might remove a useful search cue.

For the overall RQ, we can see our answer in the interaction coefficients. If either of them is significant, then we have reason to reject the null hypothesis (that there is no difference between conditions in the effect of number of characters on visual search).

And if we want to really drive this home, we can do an test of both of the interaction terms jointly, as a whole, by comparing our model to a model without the interaction.

mod_wally_noint <- 
  lmer(TOTAL_FIXATIONS ~ 1 + n_chars + group +
       (1 + n_chars | ppt) + 
       (1 + group | scene),  
     data = wally)


anova(mod_wally_noint, mod_wally)

Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

It’s significant, which gives us our ability to say that there is a significant difference between conditions in the effect of number of characters on visual search!

And in relation to our specific predictions:

Prediction 1 is supported by the significant and positive coefficient for n_chars, showing fixations increase (less efficient searching) with more characters in the standard condition

Prediction 2 is supported by the interaction coefficient for n_chars:groupgridoverlay, which is significant and negative, meaning the effect of n_chars is smaller than it is in the standard condition

Prediction 3 is not supported - the interaction for n_chars:griddesaturated is negative and significant. it actually suggests the opposite direction of the prediction - desaturation appears to reduce the effect of scene-busyness on search efficiency.
